takeaways: Select by workload and constraints, not by launch blogs.
Use the matrix as a starting hypothesis.
Measure on your data; keep historical eval versions.

body.text: Why this matters
Model selection fails when teams chase leaderboards. Workloads differ. This manual teaches a decision framework. It is not a permanent ranking of brands.

body.caption: Start from workload, not from hype.
body.alt: Start from workload, not from hype.

body.text: Decision framework

items: Does the step need to generate novel text/code/images?
If no: consider decision models / classifiers / rankers.
If yes: does it need deep multi-step reasoning?
If yes: reasoning model. If no: fast/small LLM may suffice.
Add constraints: latency SLO, privacy, tool use, modality, offline/on-prem.
Measure on your golden set before committing.

body.text: Selection matrix
Evaluation dimensions
Production recommendations
Keep a written model policy. Version it. Revisit when providers change defaults. Prefer explicit model ids over moving aliases in production paths that encode thresholds.
Conclusion

The right model is the cheapest model that meets a measured quality bar under your latency and risk constraints — sometimes that is Jev-like, sometimes it is a frontier reasoner, often it is both in one system.

Worked example 1: define the user journey, list each decision or generation step, assign a candidate model type from the matrix, write the metric, and only then pick a vendor. Skipping the matrix step is how organisations accidentally spend premium reasoning tokens on boolean gates. Document the owner of each step so model policy changes have a human inbox. Re-run a fixed eval harness monthly; store results beside the policy document. If a step is both generative and decisive, split it. If a step is high volume, invest in calibration. If a step is irreversible, invest in false-negative analysis and human escalation UX — not only in model IQ.

faqs.q: Which model should I evaluate for my workload?
faqs.a: Map each step through the matrix, then shortlist one decision-model candidate and one generative candidate where relevant. Run both on a labelled sample before standardising.
